stories.headline: OIL AND TREASURY YIELDS JUMP AS TRADERS DOUBT FRIDAY'S HORMUZ DEADLINE WILL HOLD
stories.body: WTI rose 2.9% to $77.29 and Brent climbed nearly 4% to $82.49 as a senior Gulf official put only 50-50 odds on finalizing the Iran-Oman shipping arrangement through the Strait of Hormuz by Friday's deadline; the 10-year Treasury yield followed oil higher, up 7 bps to 4.67%.
stories.explain: The Strait of Hormuz carries roughly a fifth of global seaborne oil, so even a probabilistic threat to it gets priced into futures immediately as an odds-weighted supply risk, not treated as a binary event to wait out. That repricing lifts expected inflation (the breakeven component of a Treasury yield), and since nominal yields equal real yields plus expected inflation, oil spiking pushes the 10-year up even though the Fed hasn't touched policy. It's the same channel that makes energy shocks harder for central banks to manage than demand-driven inflation — rate hikes don't reopen a shipping lane.

stories.headline: S&P 500 SLIPS 0.18% AS AI MEMORY-CHIP SELLOFF DRAGS NASDAQ LOWER, EVEN AS DOW TOUCHES A RECORD
stories.body: The S&P 500 closed at 7,709.96, down 0.18%, while the Nasdaq 100 fell about 0.6% after Sandisk plunged nearly 11% and Western Digital dove 15% on in-line guidance despite both beating earnings estimates; the Dow hit a fresh intraday record before fading to close down 464 points (-0.85%).
stories.explain: This is a market pricing guidance, not results — Sandisk and Western Digital both beat on revenue and EPS, but investors sold anyway because forward outlooks merely met rather than exceeded already-elevated expectations. When a sector has run hard on an AI-demand narrative, 'in-line' reads as disappointing because the stock price already embeds an upside surprise. The Dow's record-then-fade pattern shows the damage was concentrated in semiconductors and mega-cap tech rather than broad-based, which is why the S&P's decline was far shallower than the Nasdaq's.

stories.headline: GOLD RALLIES TOWARD $4,300, EXTENDING NEARLY 6% WEEKLY GAIN ON SOFTER FED-HIKE ODDS
stories.body: Gold climbed 2.7% to roughly $4,296 an ounce, its fourth straight gaining session, after a weaker-than-expected ADP private payrolls report reduced the market-implied odds of a September Fed rate hike.
stories.explain: Gold pays no yield, so its opportunity cost falls whenever the expected path of interest rates falls — a weak jobs print lowers hike odds, which lowers expected real rates, which makes holding non-yielding gold relatively more attractive. The move also reflects a hedge against today's oil-driven inflation risk: gold is one of the few assets that can rally on both 'the Fed may ease' and 'inflation risk is rising' simultaneously, which is exactly the mixed signal the market got today between the ADP miss and the Hormuz-driven oil spike.

stories.headline: WEAK ADP REPORT COLLIDES WITH OIL-DRIVEN INFLATION RISK, MUDDYING THE FED'S SEPTEMBER PATH
stories.body: A softer-than-forecast ADP private payrolls report initially pointed toward reduced odds of a September rate hike, but the same-day surge in oil and Treasury yields reintroduced an inflation-risk counterweight, leaving swaps markets split on the Fed's next move.
stories.explain: The Fed's dual mandate forces it to weigh a labor-market signal (ADP, pointing toward easier policy) against a supply-side inflation signal (oil, pointing toward tighter policy) that are moving in opposite policy directions on the same day. This is the textbook setup where the central bank has no clean instrument: cutting rates to support a softening labor market risks validating the oil-driven inflation impulse, while holding or hiking to fight that inflation risk further slows a labor market that's already cooling. Next week's CPI print becomes the tie-breaker traders will watch most closely.

stories.headline: 84% OF S&P 500 COMPANIES HAVE BEATEN Q2 ESTIMATES, BUT THE MARKET IS PUNISHING ANYTHING SHORT OF UPSIDE GUIDANCE
stories.body: More than 84% of S&P 500 companies that have reported second-quarter results have beaten Wall Street estimates, per FactSet, an unusually strong beat rate — yet today's Sandisk and Western Digital reactions show investors are selling stocks that merely meet elevated forward expectations.
stories.explain: A high beat rate on trailing results tells you little about forward stock performance once a sector's valuation already prices in continued upside surprises; the market has effectively moved the bar from 'beat estimates' to 'beat estimates and raise guidance meaningfully.' This is a classic late-cycle earnings-season pattern — beat rates stay elevated while price reactions to those beats get harsher, because expectations embedded in valuation are rising faster than the estimates themselves.

stories.headline: 30 MORE ATHLETES GRANTED ELIGIBILITY AS PLAINTIFFS WIN GEORGIA 5-IN-5 LAWSUIT AGAINST THE NCAA
stories.body: A federal ruling in the Georgia 5-in-5 eligibility lawsuit granted 30 more athletes an extra year of eligibility, with Jamichael Stillwell (now at Texas Tech) and RJ Godfrey (Arizona) already landing at new schools while Chauncy Wiggins remains in the transfer portal. Separately, ESPN announced the field for the 2026 ESPN Events Invitational at Walt Disney World, including Boston College.

stories.headline: TRAIL BLAZERS LAND JA MORANT IN TRADE WITH GRIZZLIES
stories.body: Portland acquired former All-Star guard Ja Morant from Memphis in a trade, the offseason's biggest move yet. Elsewhere, Draymond Green re-signed with Golden State on a one-year, $27.7 million deal, and the Wizards are among four teams — with Miami, Denver and Cleveland — in talks with free agent DeMar DeRozan.

stories.headline: JONATHAN TAYLOR SIGNS LARGEST-EVER THIRD CONTRACT FOR A RUNNING BACK IN $44M COLTS EXTENSION
stories.body: Jonathan Taylor agreed to a two-year, $44 million extension with the Colts ($47M max value, $39M guaranteed) — the biggest third contract in RB history — a day after Lions RB Jahmyr Gibbs signed his own extension. Both moves come as all 32 teams are in training camp ahead of tonight's Hall of Fame Game between the Cardinals and Panthers (8 PM ET, Canton, Ohio).

stories.headline: INDIANA OPENS AS PRESEASON NO. 1 IN COACHES POLL, CHASING A REPEAT NATIONAL TITLE
stories.body: USA Today's preseason Coaches Poll Top 25 has defending champion Indiana at No. 1 for the 2026 season, with Ohio State, Notre Dame, Miami and Oregon positioned as the top challengers. Ohio State returns QB Julian Sayin, WR Jeremiah Smith and RB Bo Jackson on what's viewed as one of the nation's best offenses.

sports.detail: No game yet — HC Jedd Fisch takes over as offensive playcaller after OC Jimmie Dougherty's February departure. Season opens vs. Washington State (Apple Cup) at Husky Stadium.

UW's 15-man roster for Danny Sprinkle's third season is set after landing Rutgers transfer Harun Zrno. The Huskies lost leading scorers Hannes Steinbach and Zoom Diallo and added ex-NBA assistant Charles Klask to the staff.

Seahawks returned to padded practice in Renton under smoky skies from Spokane-area wildfires. Entire 2026 draft class is now signed after Jadarian Price's deal; TE Elijah Arroyo has been the camp standout.

Contract talks with C Jalen Duren remain stalled — he's seeking a 5-yr/$287M max deal, Detroit is offering closer to the 25% max tier. Coming off a 60-win season, resolution expected nearer the Oct. 1 deadline.
Beat the Tigers 4-2 — Julio Rodríguez and Colt Emerson homered, Bryan Woo threw seven scoreless innings. Series with Detroit continues at T-Mobile Park.

watchlist: Iran-Oman Strait of Hormuz shipping deal — a Gulf official puts only 50-50 odds on finalizing by Friday; oil and yields hinge on the outcome
NFL Hall of Fame Game tonight — Cardinals vs. Panthers, 8 PM ET, Canton, Ohio — unofficial kickoff to the 2026 season
CPI print next week will be the tie-breaker for the Fed's September decision after today's conflicting ADP and oil signals
Jalen Duren-Pistons contract talks — no long-term deal yet, decision looms ahead of the Oct. 1 restricted free agency deadline

deepDive.title: Why Oil Shocks Move Bond Yields: Breakevens, the Fed, and Today's Hormuz Repricing
content: Today's price action is a live lesson in a mechanism finance students read about in textbooks and rarely see play out this cleanly in one session. WTI climbed roughly 2.9% and the 10-year Treasury yield jumped about 7 basis points to 4.67% off the same catalyst — a Gulf official putting only 50-50 odds on finalizing the Iran-Oman shipping arrangement through the Strait of Hormuz by Friday's deadline. Oil and long-bond yields don't always move together, but when the shared driver is a supply-side energy shock, the correlation turns tight and mechanical, and that's worth understanding rather than just observing.

The link runs through the Fisher equation: a nominal Treasury yield equals a real yield plus expected inflation. Oil feeds CPI directly through gasoline and heating costs, and indirectly through transport and input costs across the economy, so when futures markets reprice the odds of a supply disruption, they're also repricing the expected-inflation path embedded in TIPS breakevens. Because the Strait carries roughly a fifth of global seaborne oil, even a probabilistic threat — not a confirmed closure — moves the futures curve instantly, and that repriced inflation expectation flows straight into nominal Treasury yields without the Fed lifting a finger.

What most people miss is that the Fed has no clean tool for this kind of shock the way it does for demand-driven inflation. Raising rates to fight higher gas prices doesn't reopen a shipping lane; it just adds a monetary drag on top of an economy already absorbing an energy tax. The 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait sent oil from roughly $17 to $36 a barrel in three months and tipped the U.S. into recession even as the Fed cut rates in response — proof that markets sometimes have to eat a supply shock rather than have policy fully absorb it. The 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine produced a smaller-scale version of the same breakeven-inflation spike.

That's exactly the tension sitting under today's setup: a weak ADP report argued for easier policy while the oil-driven yield jump argued for caution, leaving the Fed's September path genuinely split in swaps pricing. Watch two things from here — whether Friday's Hormuz deadline actually produces a finalized deal (removing the risk premium) or slips again (extending it), and next week's CPI print, which will show whether today's oil move has started translating into the kind of headline inflation number the Fed can't wave away.
